doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Jazz education today and the loss of individuality
summary: Katz laments that students have skills but no individuality and criticizes scale-based modal teaching; Lester Young barely knew chords.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Yeah. Which blows my mind now, you know like I teach at Manhattan School of Music. And what these kids have today, available to them, I could sit you here all day and talk about the whole education scene, IAJE and the whole thing.
Where are these people going to play this? I went to the last convention, seven thousand.
I know I went too. It was like overwhelming.
It’s bigger than what they’re training for.
And all the musicians, it seems like all the jazz musicians, either by choice or necessity, have their educational part of what they do, because that’s where the money is.

And for many it’s the main thing. For instance a terrific pianist named Harold Danko, who is a full time professor at Eastman jazz, I took over his course at Manhattan School, this one course. The main part of his career is teaching now, because that’s security. There comes a point when, if you’re not a traveling musician now, and part of a permanent group, you either have to be a marketed star, made a star by the marketing mostly, and all that goes with that a manager and a record contract and the publicity and the whole thing, and then you get your group or not a group, you’re either that or you’re part of a group, or you teach. There’s very few. You know there’s Monty Alexander, there are a few musicians who make a living just traveling. But I’m beginning to think they’re the minority and I don’t really know, but the vast majority of musicians, mostly white incidentally, are in the education field. It’s a huge industry now.
And as you said what is the product they’re turning out?

I don’t know where these kids can play. And I mean to editorialize about it, the one thing that’s changed from when I was coming up it was essential that you find your own personality somehow. Eclectic or not, you had to be recognizable. Now I can’t tell — there are a few really talented individuals out there, but the rest are like — like the whole society.
Is that because of all the tools they have available?

It’s the tools and it’s the culture. There is no emphasis on individuality anymore as a prized thing to strive for. Skills are it. Skills and versatility. I’m being — it’s a big assumption on my part but I would think that would go into many, many areas outside of music, in the corporate world and everything, there’s always a place — if the guy has got some real ideas, yeah, he’ll be all right. But the pressure to conform is very strong. The way they teach modal jazz, you learn your scales, yeah, and you find out which fourth chords will go with it, and if you’ve got the chops you’ve got instant solos. See? Where the real artists don’t approach it that way, including McCoy Tyner and Chick Corea. They don’t think “I’m playing a Lydian in M-1 now go on to this.” They’re composing on the spot. The people I admire are composers, instant composers. And that means you

have to know how to develop an idea. You may or may not involve modal harmony. I don’t think Miles sat around doing that when they made “Kind of Blue” you know? Bill Evans was a very intellectual musicians and he knew — yes he knew about that — but that wasn’t his whole thing. All right so —

I agree because sometimes I look at the transcribed solos in some of the magazines you know and they analyze just about every note and how it related to the chord and look how this augmented ninth was — and I cannot believe that the players were thinking that.

No. That’s — Lester Young barely knew chords. In other words, yes, it’s a valuable tool if you have an artistic sensibility to know what to do with it, great. But if you don’t you’re a mechanic. That’s the cynical view.
